description: Somos Unreal Coders, un equipo de seis estudiantes de Ingeniería en Software y Tecnologías Emergentes de UABC Ensenada. Participamos en el NASA Space Apps Challenge, combinando programación, análisis de datos, e inteligencia artificial para desarrollar soluciones innovadoras, creativas y útiles.
summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is a web app that helps a crew member log their health indicators, understand their status, and know what to do when a reading falls outside the normal range. It covers nine indicators: the six named in the challenge (heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood) plus oxygen saturation, immune symptoms, and exercise. Each reading is rated green, yellow, or red by documented rules, not a black box. The rules live in one sourced sheet per indicator, built from NASA’s Human Research Program and NASA-STD-3001, with clinical guidelines only where NASA gives no value. Because Mars missions bring one-way communication delays of up to 20 minutes, every indicator also tells the crew when to contact the flight surgeon and what to do without real-time contact. Charts make gradual deterioration visible, and a space garden rewards keeping up the logging routine, never specific values. The app runs in the browser with no backend, uses synthetic demo data, and is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does. Astronaut Health Monitor is a browser-based tool that lets a crew member log nine health indicators, see a clear status for each one, and learn what to do next. The six indicators named in the challenge are heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood. The team added oxygen saturation, immune symptoms, and exercise. A health wheel shows every indicator at a glance, a detail screen shows history charts and guidance, and an escalation alert says when to contact the flight surgeon and what to do if there is no real-time contact.

How it works. Each indicator has one YAML sheet that holds everything medical: why it is measured, how to check it on board, thresholds, actions, limitations, and sources. The app loads and validates the sheets at build time, so a broken sheet fails the build. A rules engine reads the sheet and the logged entries and returns green, yellow, or red; no medical threshold is written in code. It also handles missing data, out-of-range typing errors, outdated readings, and values no source can rate, which are referred to the flight surgeon. Sources come first from NASA’s Human Research Program, NASA-STD-3001, and NASA OCHMO technical briefs, and only where NASA gives no value from AHA, CDC, MedlinePlus, and the PHQ-2 screener.

Benefits and impact. On a Mars mission, messages take up to 20 minutes each way, so the crew must assess their own health. The app gives them a clear, traceable guide without diagnosing or replacing the flight surgeon. History charts make a gradual deterioration visible, and every value can be traced to its source, so any result can be checked and defended.

Creativity. We chose indicators an astronaut can check alone in about two minutes: exercise replaces bone density scans, and a symptom checklist replaces lab immune biomarkers. A space garden grows with the logging routine, never with the values, so nothing rewards hiding a reading. Status always combines color, icon, and text, and chart points also change shape, so it never depends on color alone.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Recharts, the yaml package, Vitest, oxlint, browser localStorage (no backend), GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions for deployment, Figma for the interface design, and Markdown for documentation. No special hardware is needed: values are entered manually.

Factors considered. Crew autonomy far from Earth, no diagnosing, plain language, and accessibility (keyboard navigation, visible focus, reduced motion, small screens). We were also open about limits: some ranges are Earth clinical references, immune symptoms have no rating rules yet, demo data is synthetic, and this is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device. AI use: Claude (Anthropic) supported the research, documentation, code, and data.
